..
Issued at 137 PM CST Mon Nov 2 2026

A long wave trough over the U.S. Rockies into the Great Plains
is moving slowly eastward. Water vapor imagery early this
afternoon shows a pair of closed mid-upper level lows embedded 
within the broader trough. One located over the northern Plains 
will shear out/open up as it moves northeastward into a more 
confluent flow. An embedded lead shortwave trough in advance of
this upper low over the Cornbelt is supporting a band of 
showers across Minnesota south into eastern IA and far NW IL. 
This shower activity is likely being aided by strong warm air 
advection in advance of an approaching warm front. The southern 
flanks of this shower activity will likely graze our 
northwestern and far northern CWA late this afternoon into this 
evening.

The aforementioned warm front extending from western MN
southeast to the lower Ohio Valley will move northward tonight.
In the wake of the warm front, temperatures and dewpoints will
likely slowly rise into/through the 60s tonight. By sunrise
Tuesday, temperatures will likely be in the low to mid 60s,
which is about 10F above the normal highs for this time of
year. Strong and gusty southerly winds will provide for a steady
feed of unseasonably warm and humid (by Nov standards) air
through the day Tuesday.

Low cloudiness will likely at least partially scatter out in 
the wake of tonight's warm front. Some breaks in the overcast or
at least thinning of the overcast should allow temps to inch
upward into the lower 70s over the eastern half or so of the
CWA, including most of the Chicago metro area. If there is a 
bit more in the way of breaks in the cloudiness Tuesday, it is 
certainly plausible that highs could push into well into the 70s
given the progged near record warm 925mb temps. 

A tight pressure gradient will support strong and gusty
southerly winds. Just how strong the winds get Tuesday will
depend on the depth of mixing/how warm temps get. Showers will
likely arrive in our western CWA Tuesday morning, this should
result in high temps "only" in the 60s and will likely limit the
magnitude of the winds and especially gusts some. Farther east
where temps will be warmer, gusts of 30 to 35 mph are likely
with some potential for some 40+ mph gusts with any more
significant thinning of the cloudiness. Time window for the
strongest winds/gusts should be mid morning through early to mid
afternoon, with winds/gusts easing as cloud cover thickens and
especially as rain spreads slowly eastward. 

As for rain chances, they will be tied to the second closed
mid-upper level low, which is noted on water vapor imagery
approaching the OK/TX Panhandle region. This upper low is
progged to move eastward today before rounding the base of the
parent trough and lifting north later tonight into Tuesday.
Strong synoptic forcing is expected as this embedded trough is
progged to become negatively tilted as it moves north into the
Cornbelt Tuesday afternoon and evening. This strong forcing
coupled with PWATs near/just over 300% of normal should result 
in a large shield of showers, some locally heavy moving slowly 
east across the Mississippi Valley Tuesday. In our area, showers
should arrive near/west of I-39 Tuesday morning, but with 
southerly mid-upper level flow, this activity should be slow to 
spread east across our CWA Tuesday. In fact, rain may hold off 
until after dark across eastern IL and northwest Indiana. Waves 
of showers are expected Tuesday night into Wednesday morning. 
Widespread rainfall totals of a half inch to an inch are 
expected, heaviest totals likely over western CWA. 

Upper level pattern across the country is progged to get quite
blocky during the middle and end of the upcoming work week. The
result looks to be the upper low over the Cornbelt getting stuck
meandering around the Midwest/western Great Lakes. Smaller scale
vorts pivoting around this meandering upper low will likely
result in periodic showers through at least the remainder of the
work week. Timing of these individual impulses rotating around
the upper low are hard to pin down. There will likely be many
rain free times in between some showery periods. 

A return to more seasonable temperatures is expected after
tomorrow's warmth. A cold front will usher in a cooler, Pacific
origin air mass Tuesday night into Wednesday. Cloud cover and
lingering rain will likely result in near steady if not slowly
falling temps Wednesday, but still a bit above the mid 50s
averages for early November. Cloud cover and some wind will
likely limit the diurnal temp swings Wednesday night through
Saturday. NBM low temps appear significantly too cool with
nighttime lows, especially Thursday night and Friday night.
Later forecasts will likely need to bump those lows up into the
40s with daytime highs inching up mostly into the lower 50s by
later this week into the first part of the weekend. 

- Izzi
